title: The Pygmalion Effect (Rosenthal & Jacobson, 1968)

youtube.title: Teachers Were Told These Kids Would Bloom. It Was a Lie #Shorts
youtube.description:
Your teacher has just been told you're about to bloom. You have no idea, and neither does anyone else, because your name was picked at random.

This is Rosenthal and Jacobson's Pygmalion study, told from the inside. In the youngest grades, the 'bloomers' gained far more IQ points than their classmates. Later research says the effect is real, but usually much smaller, and the original test had serious flaws.

Whose expectations are YOU living up to, or down to? Tell me in the comments.

Sources:
- Rosenthal, R., & Jacobson, L. (1968). Pygmalion in the Classroom: Teacher Expectation and Pupils' Intellectual Development. Holt, Rinehart & Winston.
- Thorndike, R. L. (1968). Review of Pygmalion in the Classroom. American Educational Research Journal, 5(4), 708-711.
- Jussim, L., & Harber, K. D. (2005). Teacher expectations and self-fulfilling prophecies. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 9(2), 131-155.

#psychology #pygmalioneffect #expectations #education #shorts

sources: Rosenthal & Jacobson (1968), Pygmalion in the Classroom: in 1964 all pupils at a South San Francisco elementary school ('Oak School') took a nonverbal IQ test presented as the 'Harvard Test of Inflected Acquisition'; teachers were told about 20% of the children would show unusual intellectual 'blooming'; those children were chosen at random.

Same study: when retested about eight months later, the effect was concentrated in grades 1 and 2; in first grade the 'bloomers' gained roughly twice as many IQ points as the control children (about 27 vs about 12 points); in the higher grades the difference was close to zero.

Thorndike (1968) and Snow (1969) criticised the test's validity for young children (e.g. implausibly low pretest scores); Jussim & Harber (2005) review: teacher-expectation effects are real but typically small, and larger for young, low-achieving or stigmatised students. The 'more smiles, more attention' mechanism comes from Rosenthal's later work (1973), so it is hedged with 'maybe'.
lines: Your teacher has just been told something about you. You're about to bloom. And you have no idea.
Nineteen sixty-four, a school in California. Every child takes a test with a fancy Harvard name.
Then the researchers hand your teacher a list. About one in five children, they say, will soon bloom.
Your name is on the list. But the list is a lie. The names were picked at random.
Nothing about you has changed. Only what your teacher expects. Maybe more smiles, more patience, more time to answer.
A year later, everyone is tested again. In first grade, the bloomers gained about twice as many IQ points.
But here's the catch. Critics found big flaws in the test. And in older grades, there was almost no effect.
Later studies agree the effect is real, just usually smaller. It's strongest for young kids, and kids others had written off.
Your teacher didn't change you. Their belief in you did, a little. Whose expectations are you living up to, or down to?
